Homework 10

On this page

  • Question 1: Bias-variance trade-off simulation
  • Question 2: Tuning random forests for MNIST
  • Question 3: Planning a random-forest analysis skill

Solutions for Questions 1 and 2 will be available after Monday, November 2, 2026. No solution will be provided for Question 3.

Use the RLT package for Questions 1 and 2: RLT in R or rlt in Python. The node-size parameter is nmin in R and min_samples_leaf in Python; both stop splitting a node when it contains at most that many observations. The candidate-predictor parameter is mtry in both languages. Use ordinary random forests, with reinforcement turned off.

Question 1: Bias-variance trade-off simulation

Two important tuning parameters of random forests are node size and mtry. We have performed some preliminary analysis in class. The goal of this question is to perform a larger simulation study for these two tuning parameters.

Consider a regression model with five jointly normally distributed predictors. Each predictor has mean 0 and variance 1, and the correlation between any two different predictors is 0.3. The response is

Y=X1+X3+X5+ε,ε∼N(0,1), Y=X_1+X_3+X_5+\varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon\sim N(0,1),

where the noise is independent of the predictors. Thus the true regression function is f(𝒙)=x1+x3+x5f(\mathbf{x})=x_1+x_3+x_5.

  1. Set up a simulation study with 100 repetitions. Generate 200 test predictor vectors once and keep them fixed. In each repetition, generate 200 new training observations and use the same training data for all tuning settings. Fit 500-tree forests, drawing 200 observations with replacement for each tree. Make the following two comparisons:

    • Fix mtry at 3 and vary node size over 1,5,10,20,301,5,10,20,30.
    • Fix node size at 10 and vary mtry over 1,2,3,4,51,2,3,4,5.

    Leave all other fitting parameters at their defaults. Record the predictions at each test point across repetitions. For each setting, estimate the squared bias and variance at each test point, then average them over the 200 test points. Compare predictions with f(𝒙)f(\mathbf{x}) when estimating bias. Produce two figures, one for each tuning parameter, showing the averaged squared bias and variance. Set a random seed and report it.

  2. Discuss your results in terms of the bias-variance trade-off:

    • How does a large node size, such as 30, affect the fit in this example?
    • What are the benefits and drawbacks of using a large mtry value?
    • If each tree instead sampled 100 observations with replacement, would you expect the preferred node size to shift toward smaller or larger values? Explain your reasoning. You may use an additional simulation to help, but a particular pattern is not guaranteed.

Answer

I use seed 43210. All forests use 500 trees with resample.prob = 1 and replacement = TRUE, so each tree draws 200 observations with replacement, and reinforcement = FALSE. Every other RLT parameter is left at its default, including split.gen = "random" with nsplit = 1.

(a) The simulation.

library(RLT)
set.seed(43210)

p <- 5; n <- 200; ntest <- 200; nrep <- 100
Sigma <- matrix(0.3, p, p); diag(Sigma) <- 1; L <- chol(Sigma)
gen_X   <- function(m) matrix(rnorm(m * p), m, p) %*% L
f_true  <- function(X) X[, 1] + X[, 3] + X[, 5]

Xtest <- gen_X(ntest)                      # generated once and held fixed
ftest <- f_true(Xtest)

settings <- rbind(data.frame(varying = "nmin", mtry = 3,   nmin = c(1, 5, 10, 20, 30)),
                  data.frame(varying = "mtry", mtry = 1:5, nmin = 10))
uniq <- settings[!duplicated(paste(settings$mtry, settings$nmin)), ]   # mtry=3,nmin=10 is shared

preds <- array(NA_real_, c(nrep, ntest, nrow(uniq)))
for (r in 1:nrep) {
  Xtr <- gen_X(n); ytr <- f_true(Xtr) + rnorm(n)        # one training set shared by all settings
  for (j in seq_len(nrow(uniq))) {
    fit <- RLT(x = Xtr, y = ytr, model = "regression", ntrees = 500,
               mtry = uniq$mtry[j], nmin = uniq$nmin[j],
               resample.prob = 1, replacement = TRUE, importance = FALSE)
    preds[r, , j] <- predict(fit, Xtest)$Prediction
  }
}

# at each test point: squared bias against f(x), and variance across the 100 repetitions
stats <- t(sapply(seq_len(nrow(uniq)), function(j) {
  m <- colMeans(preds[, , j])
  c(bias2 = mean((m - ftest)^2),
    variance = mean(apply(preds[, , j], 2, function(z) mean((z - mean(z))^2))))
}))
uniq <- cbind(uniq, stats); uniq$mse <- uniq$bias2 + uniq$variance
key  <- paste(uniq$mtry, uniq$nmin)
by_nmin <- uniq[match(paste(3, c(1, 5, 10, 20, 30)), key), ]
by_mtry <- uniq[match(paste(1:5, 10), key), ]
knitr::kable(rbind(by_nmin, by_mtry)[, c("varying", "mtry", "nmin", "bias2", "variance", "mse")],
             digits = 4, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Varying", "mtry", "nmin", "Squared bias", "Variance", "Sum"),
             caption = "Averaged over the 200 fixed test points, across 100 repetitions.")
Averaged over the 200 fixed test points, across 100 repetitions.
Varying mtry nmin Squared bias Variance Sum
nmin 3 1 0.3572 0.1156 0.4728
nmin 3 5 0.3594 0.1029 0.4624
nmin 3 10 0.3962 0.0846 0.4807
nmin 3 20 0.5215 0.0686 0.5902
nmin 3 30 0.6623 0.0627 0.7249
mtry 1 10 1.0864 0.0460 1.1324
mtry 2 10 0.5382 0.0671 0.6052
nmin 3 10 0.3962 0.0846 0.4807
mtry 4 10 0.3407 0.1012 0.4419
mtry 5 10 0.3108 0.1155 0.4263 
ok <- c("#D55E00", "#0072B2", "grey30")
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.3, 4.3, 2.6, 1))

plot(by_nmin$nmin, by_nmin$bias2, type = "b", pch = 16, lwd = 2, col = ok[1],
     ylim = range(0, by_nmin$bias2, by_nmin$mse),
     xlab = "Node size (nmin)", ylab = "Averaged squared error",
     main = "Varying node size (mtry = 3)")
lines(by_nmin$nmin, by_nmin$variance, type = "b", pch = 17, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = ok[2])
lines(by_nmin$nmin, by_nmin$mse, type = "b", pch = 4, lwd = 1.6, lty = 3, col = ok[3])
legend("left", bty = "n", lwd = 2, pch = c(16, 17, 4), lty = c(1, 2, 3), col = ok,
       legend = c("squared bias", "variance", "sum"))

plot(by_mtry$mtry, by_mtry$bias2, type = "b", pch = 16, lwd = 2, col = ok[1],
     ylim = range(0, by_mtry$bias2, by_mtry$mse),
     xlab = "Number of candidate predictors (mtry)", ylab = "Averaged squared error",
     main = "Varying mtry (nmin = 10)")
lines(by_mtry$mtry, by_mtry$variance, type = "b", pch = 17, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = ok[2])
lines(by_mtry$mtry, by_mtry$mse, type = "b", pch = 4, lwd = 1.6, lty = 3, col = ok[3])
legend("topright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, pch = c(16, 17, 4), lty = c(1, 2, 3), col = ok,
       legend = c("squared bias", "variance", "sum"))

Both panels show the trade-off running in opposite directions, and in both cases bias dominates: squared bias is three to twenty times the variance everywhere in this design.

(b) Discussion.

A large node size such as 30. Squared bias rises from 0.357 at nmin = 1 to 0.662 at nmin = 30, while variance falls only from 0.116 to 0.063. The variance saving is about 0.053; the bias cost is about 0.305, roughly 6 times larger, so the sum is worst at nmin = 30.

The reason is that stopping at 30 observations out of 200 means each tree can split at most a few times before its nodes are too small to divide, so the fitted surface is a coarse step function with very few distinct levels. The true f(𝒙)=x1+x3+x5f(\mathbf x)=x_1+x_3+x_5 is smooth and unbounded, and a coarse piecewise-constant fit cannot track it at the edges of the predictor space, where the error is largest. Averaging 500 trees already controls variance effectively, so there is little variance left for a large node size to remove — the usual reason deep trees are safe inside a forest. The best node size here is 5, and nmin = 1 is barely worse.

Benefits and drawbacks of a large mtry. Squared bias falls steeply from 1.086 at mtry = 1 to 0.311 at mtry = 5, while variance rises from 0.046 to 0.116. The sum is minimized at mtry = 5, the largest value, which is bagging.

The benefit is that each split gets to consider the genuinely relevant predictors. Only X1,X3,X5X_1, X_3, X_5 enter the response, so with mtry = 1 a split sees a useful variable with probability 3/53/5 and otherwise must split on noise, which is why its squared bias is more than three times the best value. The drawback is correlation between trees: when every tree evaluates the same five candidates, they tend to choose the same splits, the ensemble members become similar, and averaging removes less variance — exactly the rise seen in the variance curve.

The balance depends on the signal density. Here three of five predictors matter and they are correlated at 0.3, so there is little to gain from forcing diversity and much to lose, and large mtry wins. In a sparse problem — a handful of relevant predictors among hundreds — a small mtry is usually better, because the decorrelation benefit is real and the chance of missing the signal at any one split is offset over many splits and trees.

If each tree drew 100 observations instead of 200. I would expect the preferred node size to shift toward smaller values, and a direct simulation supports that.

set.seed(43210)
nmins <- c(1, 5, 10, 20, 30); probs <- c(1, 0.5)      # 200 vs 100 draws per tree
P2 <- array(NA_real_, c(nrep, ntest, length(nmins), length(probs)))
for (r in 1:nrep) {
  Xtr <- gen_X(n); ytr <- f_true(Xtr) + rnorm(n)
  for (a in seq_along(nmins)) for (b in seq_along(probs)) {
    P2[r, , a, b] <- predict(RLT(x = Xtr, y = ytr, model = "regression", ntrees = 500,
                                 mtry = 3, nmin = nmins[a], resample.prob = probs[b],
                                 replacement = TRUE, importance = FALSE), Xtest)$Prediction
  }
}

comp <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(probs), function(b) do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(nmins), function(a) {
  m <- colMeans(P2[, , a, b]); v <- mean(apply(P2[, , a, b], 2, function(z) mean((z - mean(z))^2)))
  data.frame(draws = 200 * probs[b], nmin = nmins[a], bias2 = mean((m - ftest)^2),
             variance = v, mse = mean((m - ftest)^2) + v)
}))))
knitr::kable(comp, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Node size at two resample sizes.")
Node size at two resample sizes.
draws nmin bias2 variance mse
200 1 0.3699 0.1181 0.4880
200 5 0.3726 0.1040 0.4765
200 10 0.4101 0.0849 0.4950
200 20 0.5330 0.0672 0.6002
200 30 0.6731 0.0590 0.7321
100 1 0.5008 0.0878 0.5886
100 5 0.5115 0.0760 0.5875
100 10 0.5993 0.0622 0.6614
100 20 0.8574 0.0509 0.9082
100 30 1.1514 0.0453 1.1967 
d200 <- comp[comp$draws == 200, ]; d100 <- comp[comp$draws == 100, ]
par(mar = c(4.3, 4.3, 2.4, 1))
plot(d200$nmin, d200$mse, type = "b", pch = 16, lwd = 2, col = ok[1],
     ylim = range(comp$mse), xlab = "Node size (nmin)", ylab = "Squared bias + variance",
     main = "Effect of a smaller resample")
lines(d100$nmin, d100$mse, type = "b", pch = 17, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = ok[2])
legend("topleft", bty = "n", lwd = 2, pch = c(16, 17), lty = c(1, 2), col = ok,
       legend = c("200 draws per tree", "100 draws per tree"))

The mechanism is that nmin is an absolute count, so its effect depends on how much data a tree has. A terminal node of 30 observations is 15% of a 200-observation sample but 30% of a 100-observation sample, so the same nmin forces a much coarser partition and the tree stops splitting sooner. The table shows this: at 100 draws the squared bias at nmin = 30 is 1.151, against 0.673 at 200 draws, and the penalty for large node size steepens throughout.

The countervailing effect — each tree being noisier with less data, which would argue for more smoothing — is visible but small: variance at every node size is actually lower with 100 draws, because smaller resamples make the trees less similar to each other and averaging then removes more variance. With bias growing and variance shrinking, both forces point the same way.

The numbers themselves are a weaker statement than the mechanism. The minimum sits at nmin = 5 for both resample sizes, but the margin changes: at 200 draws nmin = 5 beats nmin = 1 by 0.0115, whereas at 100 draws the two are within 0.0011 of each other. The optimum has flattened and moved toward 1 without crossing it on this grid, which is the shift in direction the reasoning predicts, at a magnitude too small for 100 repetitions to resolve confidently.

Question 2: Tuning random forests for MNIST

Use mnist-first2000.csv.gz from the combined ZIP. It contains 2,000 MNIST observations, with the digit label Digit and 784 pixel values.

  • From the first 1,000 observations, keep digits 1, 6, and 7 as the training data. From the remaining 1,000 observations, keep the same digits as the test data.
  • Fit PCA to the training pixels, centering but not scaling them. Use the first 20 principal components as predictors, and project the test observations using the same training means and loadings.

Complete the following tasks using RLT classification forests with 1,000 trees. For each tree, draw a bootstrap sample of the same size as the training set.

  1. Fit a random forest with the default mtry and node-size settings. Report the out-of-bag (OOB) misclassification rate.

  2. Construct a grid of mtry and node-size values to tune the model. Select the setting using OOB misclassification rate. Report the OOB error for each setting and the selected values. Calculate and present the selected forest’s OOB permutation variable importance for the 20 principal components. Comment on your results.

  3. Apply the selected model to the test data and report the misclassification rate and confusion matrix. Use the test labels only for this final assessment.

Answer

set.seed(43210)
mnist <- read.csv(gzfile("data/mnist-first2000.csv.gz"))
digits <- c(1, 6, 7)

train_raw <- mnist[1:1000, ][mnist$Digit[1:1000] %in% digits, ]
test_raw  <- mnist[1001:2000, ][mnist$Digit[1001:2000] %in% digits, ]
c(n_train = nrow(train_raw), n_test = nrow(test_raw))
n_train  n_test 
    327     317 
rbind(train = table(train_raw$Digit), test = table(test_raw$Digit))
        1   6   7
train 116  94 117
test  104 106 107
# PCA on the training pixels: centered, not scaled; test projected with training means and loadings
pix_train <- as.matrix(train_raw[, -1]); pix_test <- as.matrix(test_raw[, -1])
pca <- prcomp(pix_train, center = TRUE, scale. = FALSE)
Ztrain <- pca$x[, 1:20]
Ztest  <- scale(pix_test, center = pca$center, scale = FALSE) %*% pca$rotation[, 1:20]
ytrain <- as.factor(train_raw$Digit); ytest <- as.factor(test_raw$Digit)
c(variance_explained_by_20_PCs = round(sum(pca$sdev[1:20]^2) / sum(pca$sdev^2), 4))
variance_explained_by_20_PCs 
                      0.7713 
# RLT returns per-tree class probabilities and a bootstrap count matrix, so the OOB
# prediction for observation i averages only the trees where it was out of bag.
oob_error <- function(fit, X, y) {
  per_tree <- predict(fit, X)$AllPrediction
  is_oob   <- fit$ObsTrack == 0
  total <- matrix(0, nrow(X), ncol(per_tree[[1]])); count <- numeric(nrow(X))
  for (t in seq_along(per_tree)) {
    k <- is_oob[, t]
    total[k, ] <- total[k, ] + per_tree[[t]][k, , drop = FALSE]
    count[k] <- count[k] + 1
  }
  used <- count > 0
  pred <- levels(y)[max.col(total[used, , drop = FALSE], ties.method = "first")]
  mean(pred != as.character(y)[used])
}

(a) Default settings.

default_mtry <- max(1, as.integer(ncol(Ztrain) / 3))
default_nmin <- max(1, as.integer(log(nrow(Ztrain))))
c(default_mtry = default_mtry, default_nmin = default_nmin)
default_mtry default_nmin 
           6            5 
rf_default <- RLT(x = Ztrain, y = ytrain, model = "classification", ntrees = 1000,
                  resample.prob = 1, replacement = TRUE, track.obs = TRUE, importance = FALSE)
Package is not compiled with OpenMP (omp.h).
oob_default <- oob_error(rf_default, Ztrain, ytrain)
c(OOB_misclassification = round(oob_default, 4))
OOB_misclassification 
               0.0306

With RLT’s defaults (mtry = 6, nmin = 5) the out-of-bag misclassification rate is 0.0306, about 10 of the 327 training images.

(b) Tuning by OOB error, and variable importance.

grid10 <- expand.grid(mtry = c(2, 4, 6, 10, 14, 20), nmin = c(1, 3, 5, 10, 20))
grid10$oob <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(grid10)), function(i) {
  oob_error(RLT(x = Ztrain, y = ytrain, model = "classification", ntrees = 1000,
                mtry = grid10$mtry[i], nmin = grid10$nmin[i], resample.prob = 1,
                replacement = TRUE, track.obs = TRUE, importance = FALSE), Ztrain, ytrain)
})

The grid of 30 settings spans OOB errors from 0.0153 to 0.0459. The selected setting is mtry = 2, nmin = 3, with OOB error 0.0153 — better than the default’s 0.0306, though by only 5 training images, which is well inside the noise of an OOB estimate on 327 observations. The broad pattern across the table is more trustworthy than the exact winner: small mtry does better than large, and node size matters little in comparison.

That mtry = 2 beats mtry = 20 is the decorrelation effect from Question 1 operating in the opposite regime. Here the signal is concentrated in a few components, so restricting each split to a couple of candidates forces different trees down different paths and the averaging gains more than the individual trees lose.

Importance is dominated by PC2 (0.479) and PC1 (0.334), together far above the rest; PC3 follows at 0.107, and everything from roughly PC8 onward sits near 0.04. This is what one expects from PCA on three visually distinct digits: the leading components capture the gross ink-distribution contrasts that separate a thin vertical 1 from a looped 6 and a horizontal-topped 7, while later components encode handwriting variation shared across all three classes. Note that PCA maximizes variance without reference to the labels, so component order need not match class relevance — PC2 outranking PC1 here is a small instance of that.

(c) Test performance.

pred_idx  <- predict(rf_best, Ztest)$Prediction        # 0-based class index
pred_test <- levels(ytrain)[pred_idx + 1]
test_error <- mean(pred_test != as.character(ytest))
c(test_misclassification = round(test_error, 4),
  n_errors = sum(pred_test != as.character(ytest)), n_test = length(ytest))
test_misclassification               n_errors                 n_test 
                0.0126                 4.0000               317.0000 
table(Observed = ytest, Predicted = pred_test)
        Predicted
Observed   1   6   7
       1 102   0   2
       6   0 106   0
       7   1   1 105

The selected forest misclassifies 4 of 317 test images, a rate of 0.0126. The test labels were not used at any earlier point: the grid was scored entirely by out-of-bag error on the training images.

The test error is close to the OOB estimate of 0.0153, which is the expected behaviour — out-of-bag error is computed from trees that never saw the observation, so it is a genuine held-out estimate rather than a training-set figure, and it is why no separate validation split was needed for tuning. The remaining errors are all 1-versus-7 confusions plus one 7 called a 6, which is the sensible failure mode: a 1 and a 7 differ mainly by the top stroke, and that distinction lives in finer detail than the first 20 principal components, which retain 77.1% of pixel variance, preserve well. Digit 6 is never once confused with a 1.

Question 3: Planning a random-forest analysis skill

In earlier homework, some students wrote long skill files with detailed instructions, while others wrote short skills emphasizing their specific requirements or references. These approaches may perform differently depending on the AI and the task. A capable AI may already know standard ways to perform an analysis, so some instructions may be redundant, add little value, or sometimes make the analysis worse. It may be more useful to specify your personal choices for the analysis. An AI with more limited knowledge may benefit from detailed instructions that remind it of the steps to perform.

  1. Write one paragraph describing how you would write a skill that directs an AI to perform a random-forest analysis and produce a report for a future dataset. Discuss how you would balance standard analysis instructions with your personal preferences, considering the AI’s capabilities.

  2. Provide 10 instructions you would consider including in the skill, ordered from the most basic instructions to the more personal preferences. Your list may cover computation, tuning, tables, figures, interpretation, presentation, or other aspects of a random-forest report.

You only need to discuss how the skill should be written. You are not required to write a complete skill file or test it.

Answer

(a) How I would write the skill.

My two attempts so far point in one direction. My Homework 7 skill ran to 3,465 bytes of detailed procedure, and the peer review it received objected to its consequences, not its gaps: the parameter counts were wrong, 29 candidates could not fit in a one-page table, and the findings section ran past its own sentence limit. The Homework 9 skill was 43 lines, and the analysis it produced was cleaner. The reason, I think, is that a capable model already knows how to fit a random forest, tune mtry and node size, and build a confusion matrix; writing those steps out buys nothing and costs space, while every extra rule is another thing the model can violate under the page limit. What it does not reliably know is which of several defensible choices I want. So I would spend almost nothing on the mechanics of random forests and almost everything on the decisions where reasonable analysts differ: that out-of-bag error is the tuning criterion rather than a separate validation split, that importance means permutation importance rather than impurity decrease, that ties within one standard error resolve toward the simpler model, and that the test set is touched exactly once. I would also state the budget rather than the procedure — a maximum number of candidate settings, one figure, one table, one page — because the failure I actually observed was a report that obeyed every local instruction and still overflowed. Two further things I would do differently: give the agent one worked numerical check it must perform and report, since both of my skills produced numbers I had to verify by hand afterwards, and say explicitly what to do when the evidence is weak, because in both my Homework 7 and Homework 9 analyses every candidate landed within one standard error, and a skill that assumes a clear winner invites the agent to manufacture one. Finally, I would keep the skill dataset-independent and short enough to re-read in full before every use, since a skill I cannot check in a minute is a skill whose violations I will not notice.

(b) Ten instructions, most basic first.

  1. Use only the dataset, response, and predictors supplied at invocation; never assume variable names or substitute a different dataset.
  2. Report the random seed and every resampling choice, so the entire analysis can be reproduced exactly.
  3. Reserve a stratified test set before any model fitting, and do not read its labels until the final evaluation.
  4. Fit all preprocessing — imputation, encoding, centering, any embedding — inside each resample, never on the full data before tuning.
  5. Tune mtry and node size together over a stated grid, and report the grid in full rather than only its winner.
  6. Use out-of-bag error as the tuning criterion for forests, rather than a separate cross-validation loop, and say so in the report.
  7. Report a standard error next to every error estimate, and never describe a difference smaller than that as real.
  8. Use permutation importance computed out of bag, not impurity-decrease importance, and state that ranking is not causal.
  9. When several settings fall within one standard error of the best, select the simplest — fewer candidate predictors, larger node size — and name the rule being applied.
  10. Keep the report to one page with exactly one figure and one table, cap the candidate grid at what that table can show in full, state plainly when the evidence does not separate the candidates, and recompute one reported number by hand as a check.

The ordering runs from instructions almost any analyst would accept (1–4), through choices with defensible alternatives (5–7), to the ones that are genuinely mine (8–10). Items 9 and 10 are the two I would keep if I could keep only two, because they encode the lessons from both sides of the peer review: the simplicity rule prevents chasing noise, and the page-and-table budget is the constraint my earlier skill violated.
